chunks: "The recipe is: pick the net, pick the instrument, hook the return up properly, then set up the instrument.
For a DC rail I put the DMM black lead on a ground pad and the red on the rail pad and read it, and compare to the expected value, maybe checking under load too.
For ripple and noise I use the scope with a spring ground tip or tip-and-barrel on the rail pad and the adjacent ground pad, AC coupled, 20 megahertz bandwidth limit.
For power sequencing I put several scope channels on the enable and rail pads and trigger on the first rail, which shows the order and timing.
For a bus like I2C or UART I clip a logic analyser or scope onto the pads and decode the traffic.

For current, I probe across the shunt's two test pads: 10 millivolts across a 10 milliohm shunt means 1 amp, measured with a differential probe or a meter on its millivolt range, or I lift a zero-ohm link and put an ammeter in series.
I can also use test points to inject: drive an enable high, hold reset, or inject a test signal through a series resistor.
The main cautions are: use the ground pad, not a far-away clip; don't slip and short neighbouring pads; check the probe doesn't load the node; and sanity-check by changing the ground connection.
For fast or sensitive nets I use special points. And I write down what I measured at each test point so the next board can be compared."
